title: Rollout-Time Intervention:Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits

paper.title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model’s current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses.
We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI) , a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy’s intrinsic exploration capacity.
RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own.
Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out.
Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary.
The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr .

The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr . 1 Introduction LLMs are rapidly evolving from static instruction-following systems into interactive agents that can collaborate with external environments to achieve goals ( Team, 2026 ; Froger et al., 2025 ) . RL has been a key driver of this shift, enabling advanced capabilities such as self-reflection and long-horizon planning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) . These advances have fueled strong performance in challenging agent settings, including mathematical reasoning with code interpreters ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , deep research with search engines ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , and complex real-world tool use ( Qian et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: RTI enables successful trajectories where on-policy and teacher-guided RL fail. Nevertheless, standard RL is limited by its on-policy nature: it mainly amplifies behaviors already supported by the current policy, rather than inducing new reasoning patterns ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . As a result, when tasks lie beyond the model’s capability boundary, successful trajectories become extremely sparse, leading to unstable training or even collapse (Figure 1 (a)). Teacher-guided methods such as LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) and OPD ( Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) can partially mitigate this issue, but their improvements remain bounded by teacher capability. To further understand these failures, we examine failed agent trajectories and find a recurring pattern: the agent often possesses the knowledge and tools needed to complete the task, but makes a small early reasoning or action error at a task-critical step. As illustrated in Figure 1 , in τ 2 \tau^{2} -Telecom, the agent must guide the user to invoke a user-side tool, yet the model may incorrectly treat it as an agent-accessible tool and repeatedly attempt to call it; in Navigation, user queries are often ambiguous, and the agent must interpret noisy POI search results in the context of the user’s intent rather than blindly treating a returned POI as the target. In both cases, a single incorrect interaction strategy can steer subsequent reasoning into a failure loop, while correcting this early decision is often sufficient for the remaining trajectory to proceed normally. These observations motivate us: if such early reasoning errors can be corrected so that the rollout succeeds, can RL learn from these corrected trajectories and thereby push the policy beyond its original reasoning limits (Figure 1 (c))? However, such intervention introduces a central technical challenge: the corrected trajectories are no longer sampled from the original policy, but generated by an intervention-induced behavior policy. This discrepancy poses two fundamental risks. First, privileged reward-side information may leak into the reasoning process, producing shortcut-driven or behaviorally implausible trajectories that could not arise under genuine task interaction. Second, intervention may induce substantial distributional shifts from the original policy. In PPO-style optimization, including GRPO, such shifts can push importance ratios beyond the clipping range, suppressing otherwise useful learning signals, while low-probability actions may yield high-variance gradients that destabilize training. To this end, we propose Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI) , comprising three components: (1) reward-aware multi-agent intervention , which employs a Validator–Corrector–Verifier pipeline to transform failed rollouts into successful intervention trajectories while preventing privileged-information leakage; (2) perplexity-based distribution gating , which filters intervened trajectories that deviate excessively from the current policy; and (3) reasoning-shift-aware token reweighting , which concentrates policy updates on critical tokens where intervention induces substantial strategy changes. Together, these components enable stable learning from successful trajectories beyond the policy’s unaided exploration capacity, thereby pushing the policy beyond its original capability boundary. Experiments on public and real-world benchmarks show that RTI substantially outperforms baselines and achieves a breakthrough in the boundaries of reasoning capabilities. 2 Related Work Agentic Reasoning for LLMs. Agentic reasoning reframes LLMs as autonomous agents that combine planning, acting, and learning through interaction ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , as exemplified by ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , tool-use and search-based agents, and workflow-oriented systems with verifiable sub-tasks ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . This paradigm requires agents to plan over long horizons, navigate partial observability, and actively improve through feedback ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods for agent training are as follows: (i) Data-synthesis-driven SFT improves tool use by generating interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning, including ToolLLM ( Qin et al., 2024 ) , ToolACE ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , APIGen-MT ( Prabhakar et al., 2026 ) , TopoCurate ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and simulation or self-evolving pipelines for multi-turn data generation ( Li et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . These methods are effective but depend on large-scale trajectory synthesis. (ii) Pure RL with verifiable rewards has also shown promise when outcomes are easy to verify. ReTool ( Feng et al., 2025 ) incorporates code execution for competition-level problem solving, Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) learns search-engine use with emergent multi-query behavior, ZeroSearch ( Sun et al., 2026 ) replaces real retrieval with LLM simulation, and ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2026 ) shows that fine-grained format and outcome rewards can support stable multi-step tool-use RL. More recently, AEPO ( Dong et al., 2026a ) further improves optimization stability under long-horizon, multi-turn tool use through entropy-aware policy updates. Teacher-Guided Training for LLMs. When tasks lie beyond the model’s capability boundary, successful rollouts become extremely sparse and the policy is rarely exposed to truly corrective trajectories. To alleviate this, recent work studies teacher-guided training in two forms. One line provides token-level credit assignment using stronger teachers, often via trajectory-level teacher-student KL to derive dense rewards ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Another line introduces off-policy successful trajectories : LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , for instance, combines offline expert data with online rollouts and uses importance sampling to handle distribution shift. While these methods can improve exploration and learning, they all fundamentally depend on stronger teacher models, making their gains bounded by the teacher’s capability ceiling. 3 Preliminaries Problem Setting. We formulate the agentic task as a trajectory generation problem. Let 𝒯 \mathcal{T} denote the set of tools. Given a query x x sampled from a task distribution 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} produces a multi-step interaction trajectory τ \tau consisting of interleaved chain-of-thought reasoning z k z_{k} , tool invocations a k ∈ 𝒯 a_{k}\in\mathcal{T} , environmental feedback o k o_{k} , and a final answer y y : τ = [ z 1 , a 1 , o 1 , … , z k , a k , o k , … , y ] \tau=[z_{1},a_{1},o_{1},\dots,z_{k},a_{k},o_{k},\dots,y] . First, reward-aware multi-agent system (MAS) intervention calibrates task-critical errors at the step level, transforming failed rollouts into successful intervention trajectories while preventing privileged-information leakage. Second, perplexity-based distribution gating filters interventions that deviate excessively from the rollout policy, mitigating ineffective or unstable updates caused by severe off-policy shifts. Third, reasoning-shift-aware token reweighting emphasizes the critical tokens responsible for intervention-induced strategy changes, enabling more precise credit assignment. Together, these components enable stable learning from successful trajectories beyond the policy’s unaided exploration capacity. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed RTI framework. 4.1 Reward-Aware MAS-Based Intervention Given a query x x , only when the entire group fails (i.e., all G G trajectories generated by π θ \pi_{\theta} receive zero reward), we invoke the intervention pipeline, an MAS consisting of a Reward-Oriented Trajectory Validator , a Policy-Aligned Trajectory Corrector , and an Integrity-Constrained Intervention Verifier . By default, all three MAS roles are instantiated with the policy model itself. Reward-Oriented Trajectory Validator The validator identifies whether the current rollout step has harmfully deviated from a valid path to the gold outcome. Given the query x x and the observable history before step k k : h 1 : k − 1 = ( z 1 , a 1 , o 1 , … , z k − 1 , a k − 1 , o k − 1 ) h_{1:k-1}=(z_{1},a_{1},o_{1},\dots,z_{k-1},a_{k-1},o_{k-1}) , the current response u ^ k \hat{u}_{k} , and the reward-side evidence ℓ \ell , it determines whether u ^ k := ( z k , a k ) \hat{u}_{k}:=(z_{k},a_{k}) is still compatible with successful task completion. Importantly, the validator is reward-oriented rather than process-prescriptive: it does not penalize suboptimal but recoverable decisions, alternative valid action orders, or stylistic differences, and instead flags only those errors that are likely to derail the trajectory. In this way, the validator detects only task-critical mistakes, matching our central motivation that many rollout failures arise from early local errors rather than missing end-task capability. The prompt is shown below: Validator prompt (schematic) Inputs. Observable history h 1 : k − 1 h_{1:k-1} ; current response u ^ k \hat{u}_{k} ; reward-side evidence ℓ \ell . Body. (i) Observable evidence listing prior turns and tool outputs; (ii) Required actions derived from ℓ \ell separated into agent-side and (for telecom) user-side groups; (iii) Hard rules : false-claim, …; (iv) Negative space explicitly disallowing invalidation due to suboptimal-but-recoverable order. Output. JSON { is_valid , error_types , diagnosis , suggest_next } \{\texttt{is\_valid},\,\texttt{error\_types},\,\texttt{diagnosis},\,\texttt{suggest\_next}\} . The validator returns a structured judgment including whether the step is valid, the error type, a brief diagnosis, and a next-step suggestion. The diagnosis explains why the current step is inconsistent with the gold trajectory, while the suggested next step only indicates the direction of repair. Policy-Aligned Trajectory Corrector When the validator detects a harmful deviation, the corrector rewrites the current step into an intervened response u ~ k \tilde{u}_{k} . The key requirement is that the corrected step should remain a plausible continuation of the agent’s own reasoning process. Concretely, the corrector takes as input the history h 1 : k − 1 h_{1:k-1} , tool schema 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , the original draft u ^ k \hat{u}_{k} , and the validator feedback, and produces a revised response that fixes the critical error while preserving the original response style, action format, and local reasoning structure as much as possible. Corrector prompt (schematic) Inputs. History h 1 : k − 1 h_{1:k-1} ; tool schemas 𝒯 \mathcal{T} ; prior draft u ^ k \hat{u}_{k} (style reference); validator feedback (diagnosis and suggested next step); reward-side evidence ℓ \ell (privileged reference, never echoed). Body. (i) “silent calibrator” specification; (ii) four generation principles— style alignment , progressive correction , leakage suppression , minimal intervention ; (iii) domain-specific requirements; (iv) explicit instruction that the intervened response must be derivable from visible history alone. Output. JSON { reasoning , tool_calls , content } \{\texttt{reasoning},\,\texttt{tool\_calls},\,\texttt{content}\} . Our goal is not to replace the trajectory with an oracle solution, but to generate a minimally corrected version that stays close to the policy’s native behavior while removing the decisive error. Therefore, the corrector is instructed to follow the visible history and imitate the original reasoning pattern. Integrity-Constrained Intervention Verifier Finally, the verifier checks whether the intervened response is suitable. Given the original context and the corrected response u ~ k \tilde{u}_{k} , it verifies three properties: (i) the correction remains consistent with the gold requirement, (ii) it does not leak privileged information, and (iii) it is still a reasonable continuation of the original policy behavior. Verifier prompt (schematic) Inputs. User query; history h 1 : k − 1 h_{1:k-1} ; tool schemas; prior draft u ^ k \hat{u}_{k} ; intervened response u ~ k \tilde{u}_{k} ; evaluation criteria from ℓ \ell . Body. (i) visibility specification (only the user query, tools, and history may justify u ~ k \tilde{u}_{k} ); (ii) four rejection criteria: leak of privileged keywords, fabricated tool result , wrong tool arguments contradicting history or violating explicitly specified parameter values, unreasonable intervention ; (iii) an enumerated allow-list of legitimate behaviors. Output. JSON { ok , reasons , diagnosis } \{\texttt{ok},\,\texttt{reasons},\,\texttt{diagnosis}\} . The verifier closes the intervention loop by ensuring that accepted trajectories are aligned with the gold path, do not leak privileged information, and stay behaviorally close to the original policy. 4.2 Perplexity-Based Distribution Gating Although the intervention verifier removes trajectories with information leakage or implausible reasoning, the accepted trajectories may still deviate substantially from the rollout policy. When an intervened trajectory has low likelihood under the current policy, its probability ratios may fall outside the PPO clipping range, suppressing useful learning signals; meanwhile, learning from such low-probability behavior can produce poorly conditioned, high-variance gradient estimates and destabilize optimization. We therefore introduce perplexity-based distribution gating to filter intervention trajectories with excessive off-policy deviation before policy optimization. (7) 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate RTI across five benchmarks. First, we construct Navigation , a multi-waypoint navigation benchmark derived from real-world map scenarios, where agents must plan routes and complete tasks by interacting with real APIs from the Amap Open Platform. Second, we adopt the publicly available multi-turn dialogue benchmark τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) and evaluate on its Telecom , Retail , and Airline domains. The corresponding RL training instances are drawn from the AReaL dataset ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . Finally, we consider Claw-Eval ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , a human-verified benchmark comprising highly diverse tasks grounded in real-world environments. To evaluate whether RTI can improve performance beyond the policy’s native capabilities, we select 20 challenging T-series tasks on which the base policy rarely succeeds, forming Claw-Eval-Hard20 , and synthesize task-specific training data for these tasks. Evaluation Metrics. We report Pass@ k k and Pass k for k = 1 , … , 4 k=1,\ldots,4 . Pass@ k k measures the proportion of tasks for which at least one of the k k independent rollouts succeeds, while Pass k measures the proportion of tasks for which all k k rollouts succeed. The p@1 is the mean Pass@ 1 1 over the four evaluations, while avg p@ k k and avg p k additionally average the corresponding metric over k = 1 , … , 4 k=1,\ldots,4 . For the publicly available benchmarks, we follow their original evaluation protocols to determine whether a trajectory is successful. For Navigation, a trajectory is considered successful if the agent invokes the direction tool with the correct parameters. Baselines. We compare RTI against: Reference models include the backbones (Qwen3-8B / Qwen3.5-9B), larger same-family variants (Qwen3-235B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B), and contemporaneous proprietary models, paired by generation: GPT-4.1 and Claude-4-Sonnet for Qwen3-8B, and GPT-5.1 and Claude-4.6-Sonnet for Qwen3.5-9B. On-policy RL baselines include GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and AEPO ( Dong et al., 2026a ) . Teacher-guided methods include OPD ( Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) and LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . Further details on the benchmarks and baselines are provided in Appendices C.2 and C.3 . 5.2 Main Results Tables 1 and 2 show that RTI consistently improves agent performance, with the largest gains on tasks where the backbone and existing RL methods struggle. Three findings stand out. First, RTI overcomes bottlenecks in domain-specific interaction. With Qwen3-8B, RTI improves Pass@1 over GRPO by 24.56 points on τ 2 \tau^{2} -Telecom and 22.00 points on Navigation. Telecom requires the agent to guide users through actions it cannot perform itself; Navigation requires it to recognize noisy POI results and refine its search before requesting directions. Corrected rollouts expose the policy to successful strategies for both failure modes (Appendix C.2 ). Second, updating trajectories with a teacher does not necessarily overcome the teacher’s capability limit. OPD and LUFFY provide additional learning signals but achieve only 26.25% and 30.00% Pass@1, respectively, on Claw-Eval-Hard20 with Qwen3-8B. RTI reaches 50.00%, indicating that its gains cannot be explained solely by supplying trajectories beyond unaided on-policy exploration. Third, RTI extends these gains to diverse hard tasks and stronger backbones. On Claw-Eval-Hard20, RTI exceeds GRPO by 27.50 points with Qwen3-8B. Although Qwen3.5-9B already performs strongly on several other benchmarks, its baseline Pass@1 on this subset is 26.25%; RTI raises it to 85.00%, 23.75 points above the strongest competing method, LUFFY. All preceding RTI experiments use self-intervention. Standard RTI achieves the strongest results, showing that corrections from the much larger model deviate further from the policy’s distribution and are therefore harder to learn from, despite the teacher’s greater capability. These findings show that self-intervention suffices to improve performance across diverse hard tasks without relying on a stronger teacher. Additionally, we supplement the experimental results on the full set of unimodal (text-only) tasks in Appendix D.6 . 6 Conclusion We introduced RTI to enable agent policies to learn beyond their unaided exploration capacity. RTI uses reward-aware self-intervention to correct failed rollouts, a perplexity-based gate to filter excessively shifted trajectories, and reasoning-shift-aware token reweighting to focus policy updates on consequential decisions. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, RTI substantially improves task success, with particularly large gains on Navigation, τ 2 \tau^{2} -Telecom, and Claw-Eval-Hard20. Training analyses show that intervention supplies successful trajectories early in training and that the policy increasingly succeeds without intervention as learning proceeds. An additional comparison using a much larger intervening model confirms that RTI does not require a stronger teacher to achieve these gains, supporting its applicability across diverse agent tasks. C.2 Benchmark Details C.2.1 Navigation: Real-world Map Routing Task Description. The Navigation benchmark evaluates the agent’s ability to construct a valid multi-waypoint route plan given a natural-language user query. Given a query x x (e.g., “How do I drive from Dajin Park to Lihui Park, and then to Yixing Temple?”), the agent must: (1) issue one or more poi_search calls to resolve each mentioned location name to its geographic coordinates, and (2) invoke direction with the correctly assembled origin, destination, and intermediate waypoints to produce the final route. The agent must respect a strict sequential constraint: direction can only be called after all necessary POI coordinates have been retrieved via prior tool calls. Tool Annotations. The Navigation benchmark uses three tools in Amap Open Platform 3 3 3 https://lbs.amap.com/api/webservice : • poi_search : Search for places by text (address or POI name). Returns address, coordinates (longitude, latitude), and business info. Parameters: address (required), region (optional city filter). • around_search : Search for POIs within a circular area. Parameters: location (lat,lon), radius (0–50000m), keyword , region . • direction : Route planning for multiple modes (driving/walking/bicycling/electrobike/transit). Parameters: origin , destination , mode , waypoints (optional, max 16 points). Evaluation Protocol. The evaluation criterion is exact parameter matching of the direction call . Each query is annotated with an order level (0–4) that specifies the visit-sequence constraint imposed by the user’s intent: Order 0 (free ordering among all waypoints), Order 1 (fixed start, free remainder), Order 2 (fixed end, free remainder), Order 3 (fixed start and end, flexible middle), and Order 4 (strict sequential order matching the query’s surface order). The matching rule is order-level-aware: for Order 0, any permutation of intermediate waypoints that yields the correct set is accepted; for Order 4, the waypoints list must match the ground-truth in exact sequence. The agent’s final direction invocation must match the ground-truth call in its origin , destination , and waypoints fields at the coordinate level under the corresponding order constraint. A trajectory receives reward = 1 \textsc{reward}=1 if and only if all fields match; otherwise reward = 0 \textsc{reward}=0 with no partial credit. Maximum interaction turns are set to 6 per episode. We report Pass@ k k and Pass k for k = 1 , … , 4 k=1,\ldots,4 . Dataset Construction. To synthesize user queries with deterministic, evaluator-checkable ground-truth routes, we adopt an inverse construction protocol: rather than annotating routes for given queries, we first sample geographically coherent waypoint sets from the map and then synthesize the natural-language query that would induce that route. The pipeline proceeds in three stages. Stage 1 – Spatially-anchored waypoint sampling. We seed each instance from a single anchor POI drawn uniformly at random from a corpus of Amap reverse-geocoding records, and issue an around_search request centered at the anchor with a 50 ​ km 50\,\mathrm{km} radius, restricted to the “scenic spots” category. From the returned candidates we retain a random subset of n ∼ 𝒰 ​ { 3 , 9 } n\sim\mathcal{U}\{3,9\} POIs, which jointly form the reference waypoint set of the instance and induce the ground-truth direction call. Two design choices are worth emphasizing. First, anchoring all waypoints around a common spatial seed enforces geographic coherence : the resulting waypoint set is realizable as a single trip rather than a random mixture of POIs from disparate regions. Second, randomizing the cardinality n n from 3 3 to 9 9 exposes the agent to a wide spectrum of long-horizon planning lengths, which is the dominant complexity dimension on this benchmark. Stage 2 – Inverse query generation and order-level annotation. Given a reference waypoint set, we synthesize a natural-language navigation query by inverse-prompting a strong LLM (i.e., Qwen3.7-Max 4 4 4 https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3-max ) with the POI names. Query-generation prompt Please generate one question that asks for a route passing through {poi names}. Feel free to make the phrasing more colloquial to increase query diversity. Output only the generated question, with no additional content. The prompt states only that the generated question must request a route passing through the supplied waypoints and explicitly encourages colloquial paraphrase to widen the query distribution. The LLM is therefore free to choose the rhetorical framing (driving plan, road-trip itinerary, weekend outing), the order in which waypoints are mentioned, and whether to add hedging or destination markers — which collectively reproduce the linguistic variability of real user requests. After query generation, we use the same LLM to annotate the order level of each instance by analyzing the query’s surface-level ordering cues (e.g., explicit “first … then …” markers indicate Order 4, while “pass through the following places” with no ordering words indicates Order 0). This annotation determines the evaluation matching rule applied to the waypoints field. Stage 3 – LLM filtering. Stage 2 produces noisy (query, reference) pairs that are not directly usable: the synthesized query may underspecify, over-specify, or paraphrase away one of the waypoints, and the spatially-sampled reference set may itself contain outliers that no human traveller would bundle into a single trip. We therefore apply an LLM-based semantic verifier (prompt shown below) that judges whether the query unambiguously requests routing through exactly the reference waypoints — with no spurious destinations and no missing waypoints — and whether the reference set is geographically plausible as one continuous trip; pairs failing either check are discarded. filtering prompt (Stage 3) You are a data-quality judge for a navigation dataset. Given a synthesized query and a reference waypoint list, decide whether the pair is valid. [Query] {query} [Reference Waypoints] {waypoint_names} Rejection criteria (any one triggers ‘‘invalid’’): 1) The query mentions destinations NOT in the reference list (spurious waypoints). 2) The query omits one or more reference waypoints (missing waypoints). 3) The reference waypoints are geographically implausible as a single continuous trip (e.g., scattered across distant provinces). 4) The query is unnatural, ungrammatical, or clearly machine-generated in tone. Output JSON only: {"valid": true/false, "reason": "..."} We further split 150 150 instances as the held-out test dataset. From the remaining pool we select 600 600 instances as the training set. Benchmark Challenges. Navigation is a substantially harder benchmark than it may superficially appear, for three compounding reasons that collectively demand multi-turn, reflective agent behavior. (i) Dense waypoint sets require long-horizon, sequentially dependent tool use. Each instance contains 3 3 – 9 9 reference waypoints, and the success criterion requires that all of them be resolved to coordinates before any direction call may be issued (a hard rule enforced by the evaluator). (ii) Ambiguous location names necessitate multi-turn reflection and adaptive re-querying. Real Amap POI names are not unique: a single literal name frequently maps to multiple geographically distant candidates, and the canonical “correct” candidate is determined by the surrounding waypoint context rather than by the name alone. A competent agent must detect when a poi_search return is inconsistent with the rest of the trip and re-issue the search with a refined region constraint. (iii) Exact coordinate-level matching as the terminal success criterion. Unlike textual benchmarks where partial credit is plausible, the Navigation evaluator scores a trajectory against the ground-truth API call by exact-matching origin, destination, and the ordered waypoint list at the coordinate level. A wrong coordinate at any of the 3 3 – 9 9 resolution steps is silently absorbed into a syntactically valid but semantically wrong route, producing reward = 0 \textsc{reward}=0 with no partial credit. A low success rate on the original benchmark does not necessarily indicate a genuine capability bottleneck. In the original Claw-Eval ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , some tasks are effectively infeasible under the evaluation environment: required evidence may be inaccessible through the available Web tools, become outdated over time, or be truncated by the context-length and tool-output limits. Other tasks contain brittle graders for which semantically correct answers may still fail. Including such tasks would conflate capability-limited failures with environment-limited failures . We therefore construct Claw-Eval-Hard20 as a subset of robustly evaluable hard tasks, paired with aligned synthetic training data. Test-set selection. We select tasks through three stages. First, we perform task-level difficulty profiling over the 160 valid single-turn T-series tasks using Qwen3.5-9B. Each task is evaluated with three independent rollouts, and tasks with Pass@3 above 1 / 3 1/3 are excluded. The remaining 63 tasks exhibit low success rates and form the initial candidate pool. Second, we audit the feasibility of each candidate under the actual evaluation environment. We remove tasks whose required evidence is inaccessible or temporally unstable, whose documents exceed the context or tool-output limits, or whose graders cannot reliably recognize valid solutions. We also exclude tasks dominated by isolated knowledge recall or standalone programming rather than agentic tool use. Third, we manually inspect the remaining tasks to verify that (i) the request is well-defined, (ii) a valid solution can be obtained using the available observations and tools, (iii) the grader matches the intended task semantics, and (iv) failure primarily reflects an agentic capability deficit. This process yields 20 tasks spanning multi-step tool orchestration, failure recovery, cross-source synthesis, entity disambiguation, safety-sensitive decisions, document understanding, and numerical reasoning. C.3 More details for Baselines We compare RTI against three categories of baselines as follows: (1) Reference Models. For each backbone we include three tiers of non-RL baselines: • Vanilla Backbone : the policy model itself (Qwen3-8B / Qwen3.5-9B) without any RL post-training, providing the raw starting point. • Larger same-generation Qwen variant (Qwen3-235B 7 7 7 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B paired with Qwen3-8B; Qwen3.5-397B 8 8 8 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B paired with Qwen3.5-9B): a much larger model from the same family, quantifying how much performance can be obtained simply by scaling up parameters. • Contemporaneous proprietary models : GPT-4.1 9 9 9 https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-1/ and Claude-4-Sonnet 10 10 10 https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-4 are paired with the Qwen3 generation as the strongest LLMs available at that time, while GPT-5.1 11 11 11 https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-1 and Claude-4.6-Sonnet 12 12 12 https://www.anthropic.com/claude/sonnet are paired with the Qwen3.5 generation as the corresponding state-of-the-art LLMs. (2) On-Policy RL. Standard RL methods that optimize the current policy using trajectories sampled from it, with importance sampling-based corrections to account for potential distribution mismatch during policy updates. In addition, we also include AEPO specifically designed for agentic RL: • GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) : a policy optimization method with group-normalized advantages. • GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) : a sequence-level RL method that uses sequence-likelihood importance ratios and sequence-level clipping instead of token-level importance weighting, improving optimization efficiency and training stability. • AEPO ( Dong et al., 2026a ) : an agentic-RL-specific method that addresses the instability caused by high-entropy tool-use decisions in long-horizon, multi-turn settings through entropy-balanced rollout scheduling and entropy-aware policy optimization, improving both exploration quality and training stability. (3) Teacher-Guided Methods. Methods that incorporate a stronger teacher model to guide the policy model during training: • OPD ( Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) : on-policy distillation whose goal is to push the student distribution toward the teacher’s. Trajectories are generated by the policy model itself, and the stronger teacher scores these student trajectories at the token level; the teacher’s token-level scores are used as weights on the advantage term, so the update signal that pulls the student toward the teacher is computed on the student’s own on-policy data. Our implementation follows the mechanism of the slime framework 13 13 13 https://github.com/THUDM/slime , computing the per-token teacher signal and folding it into the advantage. • LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) : an off-policy RL approach that augments the policy’s own rollouts with teacher-generated trajectories. Concretely, whenever an entire rollout group fails—all trajectories in the group receive zero reward—we replace the failed group with successful trajectories generated by the stronger teacher model on the same task, so that the policy can still obtain positive learning signals on tasks beyond its unaided capability. D.5 Visualization Evidence for Reasoning-Shift-Aware Token Reweighting The reasoning-shift reweighting mechanism is designed to emphasize tokens whose conditional likelihood changes substantially when the prefix is switched from the rollout prompt p roll p_{\mathrm{roll}} to the correction prompt p cal p_{\mathrm{cal}} . To illustrate what this mechanism highlights in practice, we provide a visualization on the τ 2 \tau^{2} -Telecom domain in Figure 7 . The darkest tokens correspond to local edits that materially alter the reasoning trajectory, such as a contrastive marker (“ Instead ”), which signals a switch in action plan; an explicit acknowledgment of an action constraint (“ cannot perform … for them ”), which corrects the agent’s role boundary; and the redirected action target (“ guide the user to re-insert ”), which specifies the repaired strategy. By selectively amplifying such tokens during optimization, reasoning-shift reweighting improves credit assignment to the decisive local edits, thereby making the learning signal from corrected trajectories more focused and effective.
